topics.content:
CULTURAL AND CREATIVE ART
THIRD TERM
WEEK 5
PRIMARY 4
THEME - INTRODUCING VALUE IN CULTURAL AND CREATIVE ARTS
PREVIOUS LESSON - Introducing Value in Cultural and Creative Art IV - Methods of Inculcating Value (Costumes and Make Up) Primary 4
TOPIC:
LEARNING AREA
Values Needed in Arts and Creative Works
PERFORMANCE OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, the pupils should have attained the following objectives (cognitive, affective and psychomotor) and should be able to:
explain values needed in our culture and in arts work.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
pictures and diagrams showing creative hard working, honest individuals and their achievements.
METHOD OF TEACHING - Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.

Scheme of Work
9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
LESSON ONE - INTRODUCTION
VALUES NEEDED IN ARTS AND CREATIVE WORKS
When values are inculcated in culture and creative art, the following are developed -
1. Creativity helps art and artist to be innovative.
2. Honesty helps artist to show sincerity.
3. Hard work helps artists to be industrious.
4. Precision help artist to be accurate.
LESSON TWO - REVISION AND WEEKLY ASSESSMENT
As stated in performance objectives or lesson evaluation.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
1. To introduce the lesson, the teacher revises the previous lesson. Based on this, he/she asks the pupils some questions;
2. Explains the characteristics of value needed in culture and creative arts.
Pupil’s Activities - Discuss with teacher some of the characteristics needed.

- To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.
- Next Lesson - Characteristics of Value in Cultural and Creative Arts II - Why Values are Needed in Creative Work (Primary 4)

Pupils to:
explain two values needed.

LESSON ONE - INTRODUCTION
WHY VALUES ARE NEEDED IN CREATIVE WORK
Arts and crafts are useful tools for preserving the culture, arts and way of life of a society.
It is also used to inform other societies about the culture practiced in a particular society.
Values are needed to -
1. help sustain the practice of arts and crafts in order to bring economic gains.
2. preserve the art culture.
3. inform the society about the culture practiced in a particular society.
4. inculcate cultural practices.
5. develop an acceptable behaviour.
6. document, preserve and promote the cultural practice of the society.

topics.title: Music: Meaning and Sources of Music and Noise, Things That Produce Sounds and Differences Between Music and Noise Primary 4 (Basic 4) Third Term Week 2 Cultural and Creative Arts
topics.content:
MUSIC: MEANING AND SOURCES OF MUSIC AND NOISE, THINGS THAT PRODUCE SOUNDS, DIFFERENCE BETWEEN MUSIC AND NOISE
CULTURAL AND CREATIVE ARTS (CCA)
PRIMARY 4 - THIRD TERM - WEEK 2
THEME -  MUSIC
PREVIOUS LESSON - Print Making: Meaning of Leaf and Thumb Print, Suitable Leaves for Printing and Creating Designs with Leaf and Thumb Print Primary 4 (Basic 4) Third Term Week 1 Cultural and Creative Arts
TOPIC - MUSIC AND NOISE
LEARNING
1. Introduction
2. Meaning and Sources of Music and Noise
3. Things that Produce Sounds
4. Difference between Music and Noise
6. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
7. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of music.
2. Explain the meaning of noise.
3. Mention at least five sources of music and five sources of noise.
4. Identify at least five things that produce sounds.
5. State at least five differences between music and noise.
6. Classify different sounds as music or noise.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about Songs and Music with Nigerian Identity, Nigerian music composers, and music composition. They have also learned about Nigerian and foreign musical instruments.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by helping pupils understand the meaning of music and noise, identify their sources, recognise things that produce sounds, and distinguish between music and noise.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Drum
2. Bell
3. Flute or recorder
4. Keyboard or piano (if available)
5. Guitar (if available)
6. Audio recordings of music and noise
7. Generator or vehicle horn pictures
8. Flashcards showing different sound-producing objects
9. Charts showing the differences between music and noise
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. 9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
3. Course Book
4. All Relevant Material
5. Online Information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Every day, we hear different kinds of sounds around us. Some sounds, such as singing, drums, and musical instruments, are pleasant and enjoyable. Other sounds, such as loud vehicle horns, generators, and shouting, can be disturbing. These sounds are known as music and noise.
In this lesson, pupils will learn the meaning of music and noise, identify their sources, recognise things that produce sounds, and explain the differences between music and noise.
MEANING OF MUSIC
Music is the pleasant and organised arrangement of sounds produced by voices or musical instruments for listening, singing, dancing, or entertainment.
MEANING OF NOISE
Noise is any unwanted, unpleasant, or disturbing sound that causes discomfort or distracts people.
Sources6 OF MUSIC
Music can come from different sources, including:
1. Human voice (singing)
2. Piano
3. Guitar
4. Drum
5. Flute
6. Trumpet
7. Violin
8. Saxophone
9. Keyboard
10. Bell
SOURCES OF NOISE
Noise can come from many sources, such as:
1. Vehicle horns
2. Generator sets
3. Loud shouting
4. Construction machines
5. Factory machines
6. Airplanes
7. Loudspeakers at very high volume
8. Thunder
9. Fireworks
10. Hammering on metal
THINGS THAT PRODUCE SOUNDS
Many objects and living things produce sounds, including:
1. Human voice
2. Birds
3. Animals
4. Drums
5. Bells
6. Whistles
7. Guitar
8. Piano
9. Flute
10. Trumpet
11. Radio
12. Television
13. Mobile phone
14. Vehicle horn
15. Clock alarm
DIFFERENCES BETWEEN MUSIC AND NOISE
1. Music is pleasant to hear. While Noise is unpleasant or disturbing.
2. Music has rhythm and melody. While Noise has no organised rhythm or melody.
3. Music is used for entertainment, worship, and relaxation. While Noise causes distraction and discomfort.
4. Music is usually enjoyable. While Noise is often unwanted.
5. Music creates a peaceful atmosphere. While Noise may cause stress and irritation.
IMPORTANCE OF MUSIC
Music helps us to:
1. Entertain people.
2. Express feelings and emotions.
3. Worship God.
4. Educate people.
5. Promote culture and traditions.
6. Relax the mind.
7. Encourage unity and cooperation.
HARMFUL EFFECTS OF NOISE
Excessive noise can:
1. Cause hearing problems.
2. Disturb sleep.
3. Reduce concentration.
4. Cause stress and headaches.
5. Interrupt communication.
6. Affect learning and work.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
A. Multiple Choice Questions
1. Music is a _______ sound.
A. pleasant and organised
B. disturbing
C. unwanted
D. harmful
2. Which of the following is an example of music?
A. Piano
B. Generator noise
C. Vehicle horn
D. Construction machine
3. Which of the following is an example of noise?
A. Guitar
B. Flute
C. Loud shouting
D. Bell
4. Which of the following produces sound?
A. Chair
B. Drum
C. Table
D. Cup
5. Which of the following is a source of music?
A. Generator
B. Thunderstorm
C. Hammering
D. Human voice
B. Fill in the Gaps
Complete the sentences using the words in the box: generator, drum, sound, noise, generator, music
6. _______ is a pleasant and organised sound.
7. _______ is an unpleasant and unwanted sound.
8. A _______ is a musical instrument that produces sound.
9. All musical instruments produce _______.
10. A _______ is a common source of noise.
C. True or False
11. Music is unpleasant to hear. _______
12. Noise is always enjoyable. _______
13. A guitar can produce music. _______
14. Loud vehicle horns are examples of music. _______
15. Both people and musical instruments can produce sounds. _______
D. Match Column A with Column B.
Column A - Column B
16. Music - A. Produces musical sounds
17. Noise - B. Human voice
18. Drum - C. Unpleasant sound
19. Singing - D. Common source of noise
20. Generator - E. Pleasant sound
ANSWER KEYS
1. A - Pleasant and organised
2. A - Piano
3. C - Loud shouting
4. B - Drum
5. D - Human voice
16. music
17. noise
18. drum
19. sound
20. generator
11. False
12. False
13. True
14. False
15. True
16. E - Pleasant sound
17. C - Unpleasant sound
18. A - Produces musical sounds
19. B - Human voice
20. D - Common source of noise
SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that music is a pleasant and organised sound produced by the human voice or musical instruments, while noise is an unpleasant and unwanted sound that may cause disturbance.
Pupils identified the sources of music, such as the human voice, piano, guitar, drum, flute, trumpet, violin, and saxophone, as well as the sources of noise, including vehicle horns, generators, loud shouting, construction machines, and factory machines.
Furthermore, pupils learned that sounds are produced by people, animals, musical instruments, machines, and other objects.
Finally, pupils compared music and noise and understood that music is pleasant, organised, and enjoyable, whereas noise is unpleasant, unorganised, and disturbing. They also learned that music entertains, educates, and relaxes people, while excessive noise can affect health, concentration, and communication.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction - The teacher plays a short piece of pleasant music and then plays a recording of loud generator noise or vehicle horns. The teacher asks pupils to describe how each sound makes them feel.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen carefully and describe which sound is pleasant and which is disturbing.
Step 2: Meaning of Music and Noise - The teacher explains the meanings of music and noise, highlighting their differences.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain the meanings of music and noise in their own words.
Step 3: Sources of Music and Noise - The teacher displays pictures or real objects that produce sounds and classifies them as sources of music or noise.
- Sources of Music: Human voice, piano, guitar, drum, flute, trumpet, violin, saxophone, keyboard, bell.
- Sources of Noise: Generator, vehicle horn, loud shouting, construction machines, factory machines, airplane, thunder, fireworks.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify the sources of music and noise and classify them correctly.
Step 4: Things That Produce Sounds - The teacher explains that sounds are produced by people, animals, musical instruments, machines, and objects. The teacher demonstrates sounds using simple musical instruments and classroom objects.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify different objects that produce sounds and describe the sounds they make.
Step 5: Differences Between Music and Noise - The teacher explains the differences between music and noise using examples from everyday life.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils compare music and noise and state at least three differences between them.
Step 6: Group Activity - The teacher divides the class into four groups and assigns the following activities:
- Group 1: Explain the meanings of music and noise.
- Group 2: Mention five sources of music.
- Group 3: Mention five sources of noise and other things that produce sounds.
- Group 4: State the differences between music and noise.
Each group presents its work to the class.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss, answer questions, and present their findings.
Step 7: Lesson Summary - The teacher reviews the meaning of music and noise, their sources, things that produce sounds, and the differences between music and noise.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer oral questions and summarise the lesson.
Step 8: Evaluation - The teacher asks oral and written questions to assess pupils’ understanding of the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the evaluation questions and participate actively in the lesson.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.
NEXT LESSON
Modeling with Paper Mache: Meaning, Materials and the Process of Making Paper Mache Primary 4 (Basic 4) Third Term Week 3 Cultural and Creative Arts
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils,
1. Explain the meaning of music and noise.
2. Mention at least five sources of music and five sources of noise.
3. Identify at least five things that produce sounds.
4. State at least five differences between music and noise.
5. Classify different sounds as music or noise.

topics.title: Modeling with Paper Mache: Meaning, Materials and the Process of Making Paper Mache Primary 4 (Basic 4) Third Term Week 3 Cultural and Creative Arts
topics.content:
MODELING WITH PAPER MACHE: MEANING, MATERIALS AND THE PROCESS OF MAKING PAPER MACHE
CULTURAL AND CREATIVE ARTS (CCA)
PRIMARY 4 - THIRD TERM - WEEK 3
THEME -  ARTS AND CRAFTS
PREVIOUS LESSON - Music: Meaning and Sources of Music and Noise, Things That Produce Sounds and Differences Between Music and Noise Primary 4 (Basic 4) Third Term Week 2 Cultural and Creative Arts
TOPIC - MODELING WITH PAPER MACHE
LEARNING
1. Introduction
2. Meaning and Materials Used for Making Paper Mache
3. Processes of Making Paper Mache
4. Objects that can be Made with Paper Mache
5. Importance of Paper Mache
6. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
7. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of modeling.
2. Explain the meaning of paper mache.
3. Identify the materials used for making paper mache.
4. Describe the steps involved in making paper mache.
4. Produce a simple object using the paper mache technique.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about Print Making, including leaf printing and thumb printing, where they used different materials to create simple artworks.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by introducing pupils to modeling with paper mache, another creative art technique that uses waste paper to make useful and decorative objects.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Old newspapers or waste paper
2. Water
3. Starch paste or white glue
4. Bowl or bucket
5. Balloon, bottle, or bowl (as moulds)
6. Paintbrush
7. Poster or acrylic paint
8. Scissors (used with adult supervision)
9. Rag or sponge
10. Samples or pictures of paper mache objects
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. 9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
3. Course Book
4. All Relevant Material
5. Online Information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Many beautiful and useful objects can be made from materials that people often throw away. Old newspapers and waste paper can be recycled to produce attractive items such as bowls, masks, toys, flower vases, and pencil holders. This art technique is called paper mache.
In this lesson, pupils will learn the meaning of modeling, the meaning of paper mache, the materials needed, and the steps involved in making paper mache, while appreciating the importance of recycling waste materials to create useful artworks.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF MODELING
Modeling is the process of creating or shaping objects into different forms using materials such as clay, paper mache, plasticine, or other modeling materials.
MEANING OF PAPER MACHE
Paper mache is a modeling material made by mixing pieces of paper with glue or starch paste to produce objects such as masks, bowls, toys, flower vases, and decorative items.
MATERIALS FOR MAKING PAPER MACHE
The following materials are needed to make paper mache:
1. Old newspapers or waste paper
2. Water
3. Starch paste or white glue
4. Bowl or bucket
5. Balloon, bottle, or mould
6. Paintbrush
7. Poster paint or acrylic paint
8. Scissors (used with adult supervision)
9. Rag or sponge
10. Varnish (optional)
LESSON 2 - PROCESS OF MAKING PAPER MACHE
1. Tear old newspapers into small pieces.
2. Soak the paper pieces in water until they become soft.
3. Prepare starch paste or glue.
4. Squeeze out excess water from the soaked paper.
5. Mix the paper with the glue or starch paste.
6. Apply the mixture onto a mould such as a balloon, bottle, or bowl.
7. Shape and smooth the surface with your hands.
8. Leave it to dry completely in the sun or open air.
9. Remove the mould if necessary.
10. Paint and decorate the finished model.
OBJECTS THAT CAN BE MADE WITH PAPER MACHE
1. Bowls
2. Masks
3. Flower vases
4. Animal models
5. Fruits
6. Toys
7. Pencil holders
8. Decorative plates
9. Puppets
10. Wall decorations
LESSON 3 - IMPORTANCE OF PAPER MACHE
Paper mache helps pupils to:
1. Develop creativity and imagination.
2. Improve fine motor skills.
3. Recycle waste paper.
4. Learn modeling techniques.
5. Produce useful and decorative objects.
6. Develop patience and concentration.
7. Protect the environment by reducing waste.
SAFETY PRECAUTIONS
1. Use scissors carefully and with adult supervision.
2. Keep the work area clean.
3. Wash hands after the activity.
4. Avoid putting glue or paint in the mouth or eyes.
5. Allow the model to dry properly before painting.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
A. Multiple Choice Questions
1. Modeling is the process of ______.
A. planting crops
B. singing songs
C. writing stories
D. shaping materials into different forms
2. Paper mache is made mainly from ______.
A. waste paper and glue or starch paste
B. sand and cement
C. wood and nails
D. plastic bottles
3. Which of the following is used in making paper mache?
A. Shoe
B. Spoon
C. Plate
D. Old newspapers
4. Which of the following can be used as a mould for paper mache?
A. Eraser
B. Pencil
C. Balloon
D. Ruler
5. Which of the following can be made with paper mache?
A. Television
B. Mask
C. Bicycle
D. Fan
B. Fill in the Gaps
Complete the sentences using the words in the box: dry, glue, balloon, modelling, paper
6. ______ is the process of shaping materials into different forms.
7. Paper mache is made from waste ______.
8. ______ is used to join the paper pieces together.
9. A ______ can be used as a mould for paper mache.
10. The paper mache model should be left to ______ before painting.
C. True or False
11. Paper mache helps to recycle waste paper. ______
12. Old newspapers can be used for paper mache. ______
13. The paper pieces should be soaked in water before use. ______
14. Paper mache cannot be painted after drying. ______
15. Paper mache can be used to make decorative objects. ______
D. Match Column A with Column B.
Column A - Column B
16. Paper Mache - A. Used to stick paper together
17. Glue - B. Object made with paper Mache
18. Balloon - C. Used as a mould
19. Newspaper - D. Waste paper modeling material
20. Bowl - E. Main material for paper mache
ANSWER KEYS
1. D - Shaping materials into different forms
2. A - Waste paper and glue or starch paste
3. D - Old newspapers
4. C - Balloon
5. B - Mask
6. modelling
7. paper
8. glue
9. balloon
10. dry
11. True
12. True
13. True
14. False
15. True
16. D - Waste paper modeling material
17. A - Used to stick paper together
18. C - Used as a mould
19. E - Main material for paper mache
20. B - Object made with paper mache
SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that modeling is the process of shaping materials into different forms, while paper mache is a modeling material made by mixing waste paper with glue or starch paste.
Pupils identified the materials used for making paper mache, including old newspapers, water, glue or starch paste, bowls, balloons or bottles as moulds, paintbrushes, and paint.
Furthermore, pupils learned the steps involved in making paper mache, such as tearing and soaking paper, mixing it with glue or starch paste, applying it to a mould, allowing it to dry, and painting the finished model.
Finally, pupils understood that paper mache can be used to make useful and decorative objects such as masks, bowls, flower vases, toys, and pencil holders. They also learned that paper mache promotes creativity, recycling, environmental cleanliness, and practical artistic skills.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction - The teacher displays different paper mache objects such as a mask, bowl, flower vase, or pictures of paper mache artworks. The teacher asks pupils if they know how these objects are made.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe the objects and share their ideas about the materials used to make them.
Step 2: Meaning of Modeling and Paper Mache - The teacher explains the meanings of modeling and paper mache using simple examples.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain the meanings of modeling and paper mache in their own words.
Step 3: Materials for Making Paper Mache - The teacher displays the materials needed for paper mache, including:
- Old newspapers or waste paper
- Water
- Glue or starch paste
- Balloon or bottle (mould)
- Bowl or bucket
- Paintbrush
- Poster paint
The teacher explains the use of each material.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify the materials and state their uses.
Step 4: Demonstration of the Paper Mache Process - The teacher demonstrates how to:
- Tear newspapers into small pieces.
- Soak them in water.
- Mix them with glue or starch paste.
- Apply the mixture to a balloon or bottle.
- Leave it to dry.
- Paint and decorate the finished model.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe the demonstration carefully and ask questions where necessary.
Step 5: Practical Activity - The teacher guides pupils to make a simple paper mache object, such as a bowl, mask, fruit, or pencil holder, using the demonstrated steps.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils work individually or in pairs to create a simple paper mache model.
Step 6: Group Activity - The teacher divides the class into four groups and assigns the following activities:
- Group 1: Explain the meanings of modeling and paper mache.
- Group 2: Identify the materials used for making paper mache.
- Group 3: Arrange and explain the steps involved in making paper mache.
- Group 4: Display and explain the paper mache model created by the group.
Each group presents its work to the class.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss, demonstrate, create simple models, and present their work.
Step 7: Lesson Summary - The teacher reviews the meaning of modeling, the meaning of paper mache, the materials used, and the process of making paper mache.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer oral questions and summarise the lesson.
Step 8: Evaluation - The teacher asks oral and written questions to assess pupils’ understanding of the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the evaluation questions and participate actively in the practical activity.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.
NEXT LESSON
Nigerian Musical Instruments: Classification of Musical Instruments and the Sounds They Produce Primary 4 (Basic 4) Third Term Week 4 Cultural and Creative Arts
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils,
1. Explain the meaning of modeling.
2. Explain the meaning of paper mache.
3. Identify the materials used for making paper mache.
4. Describe the steps involved in making paper mache.
5. Produce a simple object using the paper mache technique.

topics.title: Nigerian Musical Instruments: Classification of Musical Instruments and the Sounds They Produce Primary 4 (Basic 4) Third Term Week 4 and Week 5 Cultural and Creative Arts
topics.content:
NIGERIAN MUSICAL INSTRUMENTS: CLASSIFICATION OF MUSICAL INSTRUMENTS AND SOUNDS THEY PRODUCE
Note: Classification of Musical Instruments and the Sounds They Produce is taught in Week 4 and Week 5, spanning two (2) weeks. Each lesson should be taught using practical demonstrations with real musical instruments, pictures, audio recordings, or videos to help pupils identify the different classes of musical instruments and the sounds they produce.
CULTURAL AND CREATIVE ARTS (CCA)
PRIMARY 4 - THIRD TERM - WEEK 4 AND WEEK 5
THEME -  MUSIC
PREVIOUS LESSON - Modeling with Paper Mache: Meaning, Materials and the Process of Making Paper Mache Primary 4 (Basic 4) Third Term Week 3 Cultural and Creative Arts
TOPIC - CLASSIFICATION OF MUSICAL INSTRUMENTS
LEARNING
1. Introduction
2. Meaning and Classification of Nigerian Musical Instruments
3. Sounds Produced by Musical Instruments
4. Uses and Importance of Musical Instruments
5. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
6. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of musical instruments.
2. Classify Nigerian musical instruments into percussion, wind, and string instruments.
3. Identify at least five Nigerian musical instruments.
4. State the sounds produced by different Nigerian musical instruments.
5. Explain the uses and importance of Nigerian musical instruments.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about Nigerian musical instruments and the sounds they produce, as well as foreign musical instruments and music and noise.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by teaching pupils how Nigerian musical instruments are classified according to the way they produce sound and helping them identify the different sounds produced by each type of instrument.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Talking drum (Gangan)
2. Bata drum
3. Shekere
4. Gong (Agogo)
5. Oja flute
6. Kakaki (picture or video)
7. Goje (picture or video)
8. Udu drum
9. Charts showing the classification of Nigerian musical instruments
10. Flashcards of different musical instruments
11. Audio recordings of the sounds produced by the instruments
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. 9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
3. Course Book
4. All Relevant Material
5. Online Information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Nigeria has many traditional musical instruments used during festivals, cultural dances, royal ceremonies, religious worship, and entertainment. These instruments produce different sounds because they are played in different ways. Some are beaten or shaken, some are blown, while others are plucked.
In this lesson, pupils will learn how Nigerian musical instruments are classified into percussion, wind, and string instruments, identify the sounds they produce, and appreciate their importance in preserving Nigeria’s rich cultural heritage.
MEANING OF MUSICAL INSTRUMENTS
Musical instruments are objects or devices specially made or used to produce musical sounds.
CLASSIFICATION OF NIGERIAN MUSICAL INSTRUMENTS
Nigerian musical instruments can be classified according to how they produce sound.
1. Percussion Instruments (Beaten or Struck)
These instruments produce sound when they are beaten, struck, or shaken.
Instrument - Tribe - Sound Produced
- Talking Drum (Gangan) - Yoruba - Deep rhythmic “dum-dum” sound
- Bata Drum - Yoruba - Strong rhythmic drumming sound
- Ekwe (Wooden Slit Drum) - Igbo - Hollow knocking sound
- Udu Drum - Igbo - Deep booming sound
- Gong (Agogo) - Yoruba/Igbo - Metallic ringing sound
- Shekere - Yoruba - Rattling or shaking sound
2. Wind Instruments (Blown)
These instruments produce sound when air is blown into them.
Instrument - Tribe - Sound Produced
- Oja Flute - Igbo - Soft, high-pitched sound
- Kakaki - Hausa - Loud, long trumpet sound
- Animal Horn - Various Nigerian tribes - Loud blowing sound
3. String Instruments (Plucked)
These instruments produce sound when their strings are plucked.
Instrument - Tribe - Sound Produced
- Goje - Hausa - Soft violin-like soun
- Kora - Hausa/Fulani - Gentle melodious sound
SOUNDS PRODUCED BY MUSICAL INSTRUMENTS
Different musical instruments produce different sounds, such as:
1. Talking Drum - Rhythmic drum sound
2. Bata Drum - Deep drum beats
3. Shekere - Rattling sound
4. Gong - Ringing metallic sound
5. Oja Flute - High-pitched sound
6. Kakaki - Loud trumpet sound
7. Goje - Soft string sound
8. Udu Drum - Deep booming sound
USES OF NIGERIAN MUSICAL INSTRUMENTS
Nigerian musical instruments are used for:
1. Entertainment
2. Traditional dances
3. Cultural festivals
4. Religious worship
5. Royal ceremonies
6. Communication in some communities
7. Storytelling and drama
IMPORTANCE OF NIGERIAN MUSICAL INSTRUMENTS
They help to:
1. Preserve Nigerian culture.
2. Promote traditional music.
3. Entertain people.
4. Support dancing and drama.
5. Teach cultural values.
6. Promote national identity.
7. Encourage appreciation of Nigerian heritage.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
A. Multiple Choice Questions
1. Musical instruments are objects used to produce _______.
A. water
B. food
C. musical sounds
D. clothes
2. Which of the following is a percussion instrument?
A. Oja flute
B. Talking drum
C. Goje
D. Kakaki
3. Which Nigerian musical instrument is played by blowing?
A. Oja flute
B. Bata drum
C. Shekere
D. Udu drum
4. Which Nigerian musical instrument belongs to the string family?
A. Shekere
B. Gong
C. Talking drum
D. Goje
5. The Shekere produces a _______ sound.
A. whistling
B. trumpet
C. rattling
D. violin
B. Fill in the Gaps
Complete the sentences using the words in the box: percussion, flute, strings, drum, blown
6. Instruments that are beaten or shaken are called _______ instruments.
7. The Oja is a traditional _______.
8. The Goje produces sound from its _______.
9. The Talking _______ is a Yoruba musical instrument.
10. Wind instruments produce sound when they are _______.
C. True or False
11. The Talking Drum is a percussion instrument. _______
12. The Kakaki is played by beating. _______
13. The Goje is a string instrument. _______
14. Nigerian musical instruments help to destroy culture. _______
15. The Shekere is a string instrument. _______
D. Match Column A with Column B.
Column A - Column B
16. Talking Drum - A. String instrument
17. Oja - B. Wind instrument
18. Goje - C. Percussion instrument
19. Shekere - D. Rattling sound
20. Kakaki - E. Long trumpet sound
ANSWER KEYS
1. C - Musical sounds
2. B - Talking drum
3. A - Oja flute
4. D - Goje
5. C - Rattling
6. percussion
7. flute
8. strings
9. drum
10. blown
11. True
12. False
13. True
14. False
15. False
16. C - Percussion instrument
17. B - Wind instrument
18. A - String instrument
19. D - Rattling sound
20. E - Long trumpet sound
SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that musical instruments are objects used to produce musical sounds. They also learned that Nigerian musical instruments are classified according to the way they produce sound.
Pupils identified the three main classes of Nigerian musical instruments:
- Percussion instruments, which are beaten, struck, or shaken.
- Wind instruments, which are played by blowing.
- String instruments, which produce sound when their strings are plucked.
Furthermore, pupils identified examples of each class, such as the Talking Drum, Bata Drum, Shekere, Gong, Oja Flute, Kakaki, Goje, and Udu Drum, and described the different sounds they produce.
Finally, pupils learned that Nigerian musical instruments are used for entertainment, traditional dances, cultural festivals, religious worship, royal ceremonies, and communication, and that they help to preserve Nigeria’s cultural heritage and promote appreciation of traditional music.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction - The teacher displays different Nigerian musical instruments or pictures of them, such as the Talking Drum, Shekere, Gong, Oja Flute, Kakaki, Goje, and Udu Drum. The teacher asks pupils if they have seen or heard any of these instruments before.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe the instruments, identify those they know, and describe where they have seen them.
Step 2: Meaning of Musical Instruments - The teacher explains the meaning of musical instruments and introduces the three main classifications of Nigerian musical instruments:
- Percussion instruments
- Wind instruments
- String instruments
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain the meaning of musical instruments and mention the three classes.
Step 3: Classification of Nigerian Musical Instruments - The teacher explains each class with examples:
- Percussion Instruments: Talking Drum (Gangan), Bata Drum, Shekere, Gong (Agogo), Udu Drum, Ekwe.
- Wind Instruments: Oja Flute, Kakaki, Animal Horn.
- String Instruments: Goje and Kora.
The teacher explains how each class produces sound.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils classify the instruments correctly according to how they produce sound.
Step 4: Sounds Produced by the Instruments - The teacher demonstrates or plays recordings of the sounds produced by different Nigerian musical instruments and explains their unique sounds.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils listen carefully and identify the instrument that produces each sound.
Step 5: Practical Activity - The teacher allows pupils to observe, touch, or play available musical instruments and identify the type of sound each instrument produces.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify the instruments, classify them, and describe the sounds they produce.
Step 6: Group Activity - The teacher divides the class into four groups and assigns the following activities:
- Group 1: Explain the meaning of musical instruments and list the three classifications.
- Group 2: Identify and classify percussion instruments.
- Group 3: Identify wind and string instruments and explain how they produce sound.
- Group 4: Describe the sounds produced by different Nigerian musical instruments and state their uses.
Each group presents its work to the class.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss, classify instruments, describe their sounds, and present their findings.
Step 7: Lesson Summary - The teacher reviews the meaning of musical instruments, their classification, the sounds they produce, and their importance in Nigerian culture.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer oral questions and summarise the lesson.
Step 8: Evaluation - The teacher asks oral and written questions to assess pupils’ understanding of the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the evaluation questions and participate actively in the lesson.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.
NEXT LESSON
Drama and Theatre: Meaning, Differences Between Drama and Theatre, and Drama Presentation | Primary 4 (Basic 4) Third Term Week 6 Cultural and Creative Arts
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils,
1. Explain the meaning of musical instruments.
2. Classify Nigerian musical instruments into percussion, wind, and string instruments.
3. Identify at least five Nigerian musical instruments.
4. State the sounds produced by different Nigerian musical instruments.
5. Explain the uses and importance of Nigerian musical instruments.

topics.title: Drama and Theatre: Meaning, Differences Between Drama and Theatre, and Drama Presentation | Primary 4 (Basic 4) Third Term Week 6 Cultural and Creative Arts
topics.content:
DRAMA: MEANING, DIFFERENCES BETWEEN DRAMA AND THEATRE, AND DRAMA PRESENTATION
CULTURAL AND CREATIVE ARTS (CCA)
PRIMARY 4 - THIRD TERM - WEEK 6
THEME -  DRAMA
PREVIOUS LESSON - Nigerian Musical Instruments: Classification of Musical Instruments and the Sounds They Produce Primary 4 (Basic 4) Third Term Week 4 and Week 5 Cultural and Creative Arts
TOPIC - DRAMA AND THEATRE
LEARNING
1. Introduction
2. Meaning of Drama and Theater
3. Differences between Drama and Theatre
4. Simple Drama Presentation with Moral Lessons
5. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
6. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of drama.
2. Explain the meaning of theatre.
3. State at least five differences between drama and theatre.
4. Identify the basic elements of drama.
5. Participate in a simple drama presentation.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about creating simple plays on honesty, integrity, and right attitude to work. They have also learned about music, dance, and Nigerian musical instruments.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by introducing the concepts of drama and theatre, explaining their differences, and engaging pupils in a simple drama presentation.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Drama script
2. Costumes (simple school uniforms, hats, scarves, etc.)
3. Props (school bag, book, chair, purse, table, etc.)
4. Pictures or charts showing a theatre and a stage
5. Flashcards showing the elements of drama
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. 9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
3. Course Book
4. All Relevant Material
5. Online Information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Have you ever watched people act out a story in school, church, or during a cultural celebration? They speak, move, and pretend to be different characters to entertain and teach important lessons. This is called drama. The place where such performances are presented is called a theatre.
In this lesson, pupils will learn the meaning of drama, the meaning of theatre, the differences between drama and theatre, and take part in a simple drama presentation.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF DRAMA
Drama is the act of telling or presenting a story through acting, speech, movement, and actions before an audience.
Drama helps people express ideas, feelings, and events in an interesting and entertaining way.
MEANING OF THEATRE
Theatre is the place or building where drama is performed before an audience. It can also refer to the stage where actors present a play.
DIFFERENCES BETWEEN DRAMA AND THEATRE
1. Drama is the acting or performance of a story. While Theatre is the place where drama is performed.
2. Drama is an art or activity. While Theatre is a building or stage.
3. Drama involves actors, dialogue, and actions. While Theatre provides the space for actors and the audience.
4. Drama tells a story with characters. While Theatre is the venue where the story is presented.
5. Drama can be written or performed. While Theatre is used for presenting dramas, plays, and performances.
LESSON 2 - ELEMENTS OF DRAMA
The basic elements of drama include:
1. Actors - People who perform the drama.
2. Audience - People who watch the drama.
3. Stage - The place where actors perform.
4. Costumes - Clothes worn by actors.
5. Props - Objects used during the performance.
6. Dialogue - The conversation between characters.
7. Characters - People or roles in the story.
IMPORTANCE OF DRAMA
Drama helps to:
1. Entertain people.
2. Teach moral lessons.
3. Promote Nigerian culture.
4. Develop confidence and communication skills.
5. Encourage teamwork.
6. Improve creativity and imagination.
7. Educate people on important issues.
LESSON 3 - SIMPLE DRAMA PRESENTATION
Title: Honesty Pays
Characters: Teacher, Tunde, Ada, Narrator
Narrator: One day, Tunde found a purse in the classroom.
- Tunde: I found this purse. I will give it to my teacher.
- Teacher: Thank you, Tunde. Honesty is a good character.
- Ada: I am happy you returned the purse.
- Teacher: Always be honest because honesty brings rewards.
Narrator: Everyone clapped for Tunde because he did the right thing.
MORAL LESSON OF THE DRAMA (HONESTY PAYS)
The moral lesson of the drama is that:
1. Honesty is the best policy.
2. We should always return lost items to their rightful owners.
3. Being truthful and trustworthy earns respect and rewards.
4. Good behaviour brings praise, trust, and happiness.
5. We should always do the right thing, even when no one is wat ching.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
A. Multiple Choice Questions
1. Drama is the act of telling a story through _______.
A. cooking
B. farming
C. painting
D. acting
2. A theatre is _______.
A. a musical instrument
B. a place where drama is performed
C. a classroom
D. a market
3. Which of the following is an element of drama?
A. Spoon
B. Actors
C. Plate
D. Cup
4. People who watch a drama are called the _______.
A. audience
B. teachers
C. players
D. writers
5. Which of the following is used by actors during a drama presentation?
A. Football
B. School timetable
C. Calculator
D. Costumes
B. Fill in the Gaps
Complete the sentences using the words in the box: costumes, theatre, audience, drama, stage
6. _______ is the act of presenting a story through acting.
7. A _______ is the place where drama is performed.
8. The _______ is where actors perform during a play.
9. People who watch a drama are called the _______.
10. Actors wear _______ during a drama presentation.
C. True or False
11. Drama is a way of telling stories through acting. _______
12. A theatre is the same as a drama. _______
13. Costumes are worn by actors during a drama presentation. _______
14. The audience performs the drama. _______
15. Drama can teach good moral lessons. _______
D. Match Column A with Column B.
Column A - Column B
16. Drama - A. Story presented through acting
17. Theatre - B. Place where drama is performed
18. Audience - C. Clothes worn by actors
19. Stage - D. Place where actors perform
20. Costumes - E. People who watch a play
ANSWER KEYS
1. D - Acting
2. B - A place where drama is performed
3. B - Actors
4. A - Audience
5. C - Costumes
6. drama
7. theatre
8. stage
9. audience
10. costumes
11. True
12. False
13. True
14. False
15. True
16. A - Story presented through acting
17. B - Place where drama is performed
18. E - People who watch a play
19. D - Place where actors perform
20. C - Clothes worn by actors
SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that drama is the art of telling or presenting a story through acting, speech, movement, and actions, while theatre is the place or building where drama is performed before an audience.
Pupils also learned the differences between drama and theatre, understanding that drama is the performance itself, whereas theatre is the venue where the performance takes place.
Furthermore, pupils identified the basic elements of drama, including actors, audience, stage, costumes, props, dialogue, and characters, and learned the role each element plays in a drama presentation.
Finally, pupils participated in a simple drama presentation, discovered that drama entertains, educates, promotes culture, and teaches important moral values such as honesty, integrity, cooperation, and respect for others.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction - The teacher asks pupils if they have ever watched a drama during a school programme, church service, or cultural festival. The teacher encourages a few pupils to share their experiences.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils respond to the questions and share their experiences of watching or participating in a drama.
Step 2: Meaning of Drama and Theatre - The teacher explains the meanings of drama and theatre using simple examples and pictures.
- Drama is the act of telling a story through acting.
- Theatre is the place where drama is performed.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain the meanings of drama and theatre in their own words.
Step 3: Differences Between Drama and Theatre - The teacher explains the differences between drama and theatre using a chart.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify and state the differences between drama and theatre.
Step 4: Elements of Drama - The teacher introduces the basic elements of drama:
- Actors
- Audience
- Stage
- Costumes
- Props
- Dialogue
- Characters
The teacher explains the role of each element in a drama presentation.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify the elements of drama and explain their functions.
Step 5: Drama Presentation - The teacher guides pupils to perform the simple drama “Honesty Pays” or another short play.
Pupils are assigned different roles, such as:
- Narrator
- Teacher
- Tunde
- Ada
The teacher demonstrates proper voice projection, movement, and expression during the performance.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils rehearse and perform the drama before the class.
Step 6: Group Activity - The teacher divides the class into four groups and assigns the following activities:
- Group 1: Explain the meaning of drama and theatre.
- Group 2: State the differences between drama and theatre.
- Group 3: Identify the elements of drama and explain their functions.
- Group 4: Present a short drama with a moral lesson.
Each group presents its work to the class.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss, perform, and present their group activities.
Step 7: Lesson Summary - The teacher reviews the meaning of drama, the meaning of theatre, the differences between them, the elements of drama, and the importance of drama presentation.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer oral questions and summarise the lesson.
Step 8: Evaluation - The teacher asks oral and written questions to assess pupils’ understanding of the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the evaluation questions and participate actively in the drama presentation.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.
NEXT LESSON
Primary 4 - Cultural and Creative Arts Mid Term Test Questions and Answers
Dance: Meaning and Importance of Dance, and Dance Performance | Primary 4 (Basic 4) Third Term Week 8 Cultural and Creative Arts
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils,
1. Explain the meaning of drama.
2. Explain the meaning of theatre.
3. State at least four differences between drama and theatre.
4. State five basic elements of drama.
5. Participate in a simple drama presentation.

topics.title: Types of Drawing: Meaning, Types of Drawing and How to Draw Different Objects | Primary 4 (Basic 4) Third Term Week 10 Cultural and Creative Arts
topics.content:
TYPES OF DRAWING: MEANING AND TYPES OF DRAWING AND HOW TO DRAW DIFFERENT OBJECTS
CULTURAL AND CREATIVE ARTS (CCA)
PRIMARY 4 - THIRD TERM - WEEK 10
THEME -  ARTS AND CRAFTS
PREVIOUS LESSON - Mode of Greeting: Meaning and Modes of Greeting in Nigeria, Occasions for Greeting, Benefits of Greeting and Greeting Styles of Different Tribes in Nigeria | Primary 4 (Basic 4) Third Term Week 9 Cultural and Creative Arts
TOPIC - TYPES OF DRAWING
LEARNING
1. Introduction
2. Meaning and Types of Drawing
3. How to Draw Different Objects
4. Materials for Drawing and Importance of Drawing
5. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
6. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of drawing.
2. Identify the different types of drawing.
3. State the materials used for drawing.
4. Draw simple objects such as a ball, flower, cup, and tree.
5. Appreciate the importance of drawing in everyday life.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about print making, paper mache modelling, colours, and elements of design.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by teaching pupils the meaning of drawing, the types of drawing, and how to draw different objects.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Drawing paper or drawing book
2. Pencils
3. Erasers
4. Sharpeners
5. Crayons or coloured pencils
6. Ruler
7. Charts showing different types of drawing
8. Pictures of simple objects (ball, cup, flower, tree, bottle, chair, etc.)
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. 9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
3. Course Book
4. All Relevant Material
5. Online Information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Every day, we see different objects such as trees, flowers, cups, chairs, balls, and houses around us. We can make pictures of these objects by drawing them with a pencil or crayon. Drawing helps us express our ideas, improve our creativity, and appreciate the beauty of our environment.
In this lesson, pupils will learn the meaning of drawing, the different types of drawing, and how to draw simple objects using basic drawing materials.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF DRAWING
Drawing is the art of making pictures, lines, or shapes on paper or another surface using a pencil, pen, crayon, charcoal, or other drawing materials.
TYPES OF DRAWING
1. Object Drawing - Object drawing is drawing things that we can see around us.
Examples: Cup, ball, bottle, chair, flower.
2. Nature Drawing - Nature drawing is drawing things found in nature.
Examples: Trees, mountains, rivers, flowers, birds.
3. Imaginative Drawing - Imaginative drawing is drawing pictures from one’s imagination or ideas.
Examples: Imaginary houses, cartoon characters, dream places.
4. Memory Drawing - Memory drawing is drawing something from memory without looking at the object.
Examples: Your classroom, your school, your house.
5. Pattern Drawing - Pattern drawing is drawing repeated lines, shapes, or designs to decorate objects.
Examples: Zigzag patterns, circles, squares, and stripes.
LESSON 2 - HOW TO DRAW DIFFERENT OBJECTS
1. Drawing a Ball
- Draw a circle.
- Make the circle smooth.
- Shade one side lightly.
2. Drawing a Flower
- Draw a small circle.
- Draw petals around the circle.
- Draw the stem and leaves.
- Colour the flower.
3. Drawing a Cup
- Draw two vertical lines.
- Join them with curved lines at the top and bottom.
- Draw the handle.
- Shade or colour the cup.
4. Drawing a Tree
- Draw the trunk.
- Draw large branches.
- Add leaves around the branches.
- Colour the tree.
LESSON 3 - MATERIALS FOR DRAWING
1. Pencil
2. Eraser
3. Sharpener
4. Drawing book or paper
5. Ruler
6. Crayons or coloured pencils
IMPORTANCE OF DRAWING
Drawing helps pupils to:
1. Express ideas and feelings.
2. Improve creativity.
3. Develop observation skills.
4. Improve hand and eye coordination.
5. Prepare for painting and other artworks.
6. Appreciate beauty in the environment.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
A. Multiple Choice Questions
1. Drawing is the art of making _______.
A. food
B. clothes
C. pictures
D. water
2. Which of the following is used for drawing?
A. Spoon
B. Pencil
C. Plate
D. Cup
3. Drawing a tree is an example of _______ drawing.
A. Pattern
B. Memory
C. Imaginative
D. Nature
4. Which type of drawing is made from imagination?
A. Imaginative drawing
B. Object drawing
C. Nature drawing
D. Pattern drawing
5. Which of the following is an object drawing?
A. Sky
B. River
C. Mountain
D. Cup
B. Fill in the Gaps
Complete the sentences using the words in the box: pencil, object, memory, pattern, paper
6. A _______ is commonly used for drawing.
7. Drawing is done on _______.
8. A chair is an example of an _______ to draw.
9. _______ drawing is done without looking at the object.
10. Repeated shapes and lines form a _______ drawing.
C. True or False
11. Drawing helps us express our ideas. _______
12. A flower is an example of nature drawing. _______
13. A ruler is never used during drawing. _______
14. Pattern drawing uses repeated shapes and designs. _______
15. Drawing develops creativity. _______
D. Match Column A with Column B.
Column A - Column B
16. Object drawing - A. Draw from imagination
17. Nature drawing - B. Draw without looking
18. Imaginative drawing - C. Draw trees and flowers
19. Memory drawing - D. Repeated shapes and designs
20. Pattern drawing - E. Draw things around us
ANSWER KEYS
1. C - Pictures
2. B - Pencil
3. D - Nature
4. A - Imaginative drawing
5. D - Cup
6. pencil
7. paper
8. object
9. memory
10. pattern
11. True
12. True
13. False
14. True
15. True
16. E - Draw things around us
17. C - Draw trees and flowers
18. A - Draw from imagination
19. B - Draw without looking
20. D - Repeated shapes and designs
SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that drawing is the art of making pictures, lines, or shapes on paper using materials such as a pencil, crayon, pen, or charcoal.
Pupils identified the types of drawing, namely object drawing, nature drawing, imaginative drawing, memory drawing, and pattern drawing, and learned the meaning of each type.
Furthermore, pupils learned the materials used for drawing and followed simple steps to draw different objects such as a ball, flower, cup, and tree.
Finally, pupils understood that drawing helps to express ideas and feelings, improve creativity, develop observation skills, strengthen hand-eye coordination, and prepare them for other art activities.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction - The teacher displays simple drawings of a ball, flower, cup, tree, and chair. The teacher asks pupils to identify the objects and explain how they think the pictures were made.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe the drawings, identify the objects, and respond to the teacher’s questions.
Step 2: Meaning of Drawing - The teacher explains the meaning of drawing and introduces the materials used for drawing, such as pencils, erasers, crayons, paper, and rulers.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain the meaning of drawing and identify the drawing materials.
Step 3: Types of Drawing - The teacher explains the different types of drawing:
- Object drawing
- Nature drawing
- Imaginative drawing
- Memory drawing
- Pattern drawing
The teacher gives simple examples of each type.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify the different types of drawing and give examples.
Step 4: Demonstration of Drawing Different Objects - The teacher demonstrates how to draw simple objects such as a ball, flower, cup, and tree step by step on the board.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe the demonstration and practise drawing the objects in their drawing books.
Step 5: Practical Activity - The teacher guides pupils to draw at least one simple object and colour it neatly.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils draw and colour simple objects using the appropriate drawing materials.
Step 6: Group Activity - The teacher divides the class into four groups and assigns the following activities:
- Group 1: Explain the meaning of drawing and identify the materials used for drawing.
- Group 2: Identify and explain the different types of drawing.
- Group 3: Draw simple objects such as a ball, flower, cup, or tree.
- Group 4: Display and explain the drawings made by the group.
Each group presents its work to the class.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss, draw, colour, and present their work.
Step 7: Lesson Summary - The teacher reviews the meaning of drawing, the types of drawing, the materials used, and the steps involved in drawing simple objects.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer oral questions and summarise the lesson.
Step 8: Evaluation - The teacher asks oral and written questions to assess pupils’ understanding of the lesson.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the evaluation questions and display their drawings.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.
NEXT LESSON
Creating Music with Solfa Notation: Solfa Names, Solfa Time Values, Singing and Playing Music with Solfa Notation | Primary 5 (Basic 5) First Term Week 2 Cultural and Creative Arts
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils,
1. Explain the meaning of drawing.
2. Identify the different types of drawing.
3. State the materials used for drawing.
4. Draw simple objects such as a ball, flower, cup, and tree.
6. Explain the importance of drawing in everyday life.
